items.prompt: In `T(n) = 3n² + 100n`, which term eventually dominates as n grows large?
choices: 100n, since 100 is a much larger coefficient than n²'s 3
3n², since n² eventually outgrows any fixed multiple of n
Neither — n² and n differ only by a constant factor as n grows
It depends on whether n is even or odd, not on the coefficients
items.explanation: No matter how large 100n's coefficient is, n² eventually outgrows any constant multiple of n as n increases — that's what makes it the dominant term asymptotically.
items.reference:
Dominant term
3n² + 100n
n² term wins as n grows
100n term wins only for small n

Why: The crossover happens at n = 100/3 ≈ 33 — below it, the linear term is larger; above it, the quadratic term takes over and never looks back.

items.prompt: A benchmark tested at n = 5 showed the linear term (100n = 500) far larger than the quadratic term (3n² = 75). What does this tell you about the function's asymptotic class?
choices: Nothing definitive — the dominant term at small n isn't necessarily the dominant term as n → ∞
It proves the function is O(n) because the linear term measured larger at this particular sample size
It proves the function is not O(n²) since a single n already bounds its growth class
It means the benchmark was run incorrectly and should be re-measured at this same n
items.explanation: Which term is larger at a specific small n says nothing about which term wins asymptotically — that's determined by which term grows faster, not which is larger at any one point.
items.reference:
Dominant term
3n² + 100n
n² term wins as n grows
100n term wins only for small n

Why: The crossover happens at n = 100/3 ≈ 33 — below it, the linear term is larger; above it, the quadratic term takes over and never looks back.

items.prompt: What does it mean, precisely, for T(n) to be O(f(n))?
choices: T(n) equals f(n) exactly for all n greater than zero
There exist constants c, n₀ such that T(n) ≤ c·f(n) for all n ≥ n₀
T(n) is always strictly faster running than f(n) in practice
f(n) is the average of T(n) measured across many benchmark runs
items.explanation: Big-O is a precise upper-bound statement: past some starting point n₀, T(n) never exceeds a fixed constant multiple of f(n).
items.reference:
Big-O, formally
T(n) ≤ c·f(n)
for all n ≥ n₀
c, n₀ are fixed constants

Why: The n₀ threshold is exactly why small-n behavior can't disprove or prove a Big-O claim on its own.

items.prompt: Why does the formal Big-O definition include a threshold n₀ rather than requiring the bound to hold for every n starting at 1?
choices: It's just a stylistic convention mathematicians use with no real technical purpose
It lets Big-O ignore small-n quirks and describe only the eventual, large-n behavior
It makes the inequality easier to prove using basic algebra tricks
It only matters when analyzing recursive algorithms, not iterative ones
items.explanation: The n₀ threshold is what makes Big-O an asymptotic (large-n) statement rather than a claim about every possible input size, including small ones where lower-order terms can dominate.
items.reference:
Big-O, formally
T(n) ≤ c·f(n)
for all n ≥ n₀
c, n₀ are fixed constants

Why: The n₀ threshold is exactly why small-n behavior can't disprove or prove a Big-O claim on its own.

items.prompt: An algorithm is Θ(n²). Is it also correct to say it's O(n³)?
choices: No, since Θ and O describe mutually exclusive growth classes
Yes — O(n³) is a looser but still technically true upper bound
Only if n³ can also be shown to be a valid lower bound
Only for algorithms that are recursive rather than iterative
items.explanation: Any valid upper bound looser than the tight one is still technically a true O statement — Θ(n²) implies O(n²), O(n³), O(n⁴), and so on; it's just not the tightest one.
items.reference:
Θ vs. O
O(f(n)): upper bound only
Ω(f(n)): lower bound only
Θ(f(n)): both — the tight, exact rate

Why: O(n³) can be a true statement about an O(n²) algorithm too — it's just not the tightest true statement.

items.prompt: What makes Θ(f(n)) a stronger claim than O(f(n)) alone?
choices: Θ requires a strictly smaller constant c than the one O allows for the same bound
Θ requires both an upper AND a lower bound at the same rate — O alone only requires the upper bound
Θ only applies when analyzing comparison-based sorting algorithms specifically
There's no real difference at all — most textbooks and courses use Θ and O interchangeably in practice
items.explanation: O(f(n)) only claims 'no worse than f(n)'. Θ(f(n)) claims the growth rate is pinned down exactly — no worse AND no better, asymptotically.
items.reference:
Θ vs. O
O(f(n)): upper bound only
Ω(f(n)): lower bound only
Θ(f(n)): both — the tight, exact rate

Why: O(n³) can be a true statement about an O(n²) algorithm too — it's just not the tightest true statement.

items.prompt: Is `T(n) = 3n² + 100n` an Ω(n³) function?

No — Ω(n³) would require T(n) to grow at LEAST as fast as n³, but T(n) actually grows slower than n³
